sources.title: Historical atlas: western plateau snapshot at 400 BCE
sources.note: Local index and all five identical/coarse Zhangzhung features decoded: 400 to 1 BCE, bounds 74.227,27.389,84.397,37.538. These are atlas metadata, not independently dated frontiers. See identities.json.

sources.title: George van Driem, Zhangzhung and its next of kin in the Himalayas (2001)
sources.note: Direct university-hosted paper, printed pages 31 to 32: western plateau polity, probable conquest 644/645 and uncertainty in older chronologies; royal marriage narrative treated as a story, not an independently verified causal account. Pages 36 to 39 distinguish later religious glossaries and disputed Dunhuang medical-language identification.

sources.title: John Vincent Bellezza, Antiquities of Zhang Zhung, Volume I: Archaic Residential Monuments (2010)
sources.note: University of Virginia/THL scholarly field inventory. Direct page extraction minimal, but full institutional indexed original read through exact queries. Introduction on mostly post-eleventh-century Bon sources; typology I.1a on stone roofs; Gekhö Kharlung A-89 and note 2 on wood sample Beta 200752. Date belongs to a loose small wood round, not all standing walls. Entire volume and subpages grouped as one work.

sources.title: Li Tang and colleagues, Prehistoric agricultural decision making in the western Himalayas (2022)
sources.note: Direct full Antiquity paper, DOI 10.15184/aqy.2022.80. Excavations section: Jiweng 391 to 208 cal BCE, Piyang 396 to 212 cal BCE, Dingdong about 348 BCE to 541 CE. Discussion/results on hearth grains and hulled/naked barley. No assignment of individual sites to documented royal subjects.

sources.title: Melissa M. Ritchey and colleagues, Into thin air: prehistoric intensive crop management in high altitude western Tibet (2024)
sources.note: Direct original research article, site descriptions and discussion sections 7.1 and 7.2. Stable-isotope interpretation of water and soil nutrients; natural influences and small sample size retained. Dingdong late samples extend into fifth/sixth century CE, explicitly outside the atlas span.

sources.title: Institute of Archaeology, CASS and colleagues, Gurugyam and Chuvthag Cemeteries in Ngari Prefecture, Tibet (2016)
sources.note: Primary excavation report translated by Anke Hein, Chinese Archaeology 16, 27 to 48, DOI 10.1515/char-2016-0003. Oxford original PDF full indexed pages 32,41,47 checked; direct PDF fetch failed. Zone II is earlier, M3 2250±25 BP and M5 2150±25 BP as reported, not silently treated as calibrated exact years. M4:9 repaired painted tray and M3 right:15 wooden basin; M4 not independently radiocarbon dated. All versions one work.

sources.title: James A. Matisoff, The interest of Zhangzhung for comparative Tibeto-Burman (2001)
sources.note: Direct Berkeley-hosted scholarly paper, author-copy pages 2 and 3: 1965 Bon-po Association bilingual dictionary; WATER entry 4 gives Zhangzhung ting. Modern Tibetan rendering supplied transparently from that verified scholarly transliteration; not a contemporary BCE inscription. This paper and its dictionary discussion are treated as one source work.

proposedOverrides.name: Zhangzhung and early western plateau communities
proposedOverrides.summary: Early western plateau archaeology and later Zhangzhung history, with uncertain royal boundaries and carefully dated traditions.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One exact indexed record; no aliases.
batchIdentityNotes.limits: Atlas span precedes secure seventh-century political narrative by centuries. Early material culture is regional, not proven royal jurisdiction. Mostly later Bon literary traditions are not treated as contemporary histories. Some sites/objects extend into CE periods, which public copy states. No invented hospital, school attendance, toilet practice, exact dynasty founder or ancient script. 2001 scholarly word sample uses explicitly modern Tibetan-script rendering, not an ancient inscription. No successor link because Tibetan Empire indexed geometry begins 700, after probable 644/645 annexation.
